results.ask: Thinking about the book as a whole, what does this opening promise a reader?
results.watch: Stays at the whole; no sentence edits or line suggestions; any other level only as a closing choice.
results.reply:
The strongest promise here is withholding. Nobody says what they feel — Mara decides not to cry, the gulls "kept their own counsel," and the one piece of dialogue is four words of nothing much. A reader could reasonably expect a book that works this way throughout: feeling shown by what people refuse to do, and a narrator who won't step in and explain.

The second promise is a third person we haven't met. Tomas is behind her, lighting a cigarette; the coat at the rail belongs to someone on the ferry. So the opening sets up a triangle in seven sentences — the man leaving, the man staying, and Mara between them, not crying in front of the one who thinks she's ridiculous. That's a lot of engine for a short paragraph, and it promises the departing man will matter.

Worth flagging: because Tomas is the only man named, some readers may attach "his coat" to him on first pass and have to correct themselves. That might be exactly the slight disorientation you want, or it might cost you the reveal. Either way it's a choice, not a problem, and I'd want to know whether the man on the ferry is named soon before I'd say anything about it.

Third, the narrator's access. The sentence about Tomas thinking she's ridiculous steps out of Mara for one clause. If the book stays mostly with her, that moment promises we'll occasionally be shown how others read her — which is a particular kind of book, one where being misjudged is part of the material.

Before I'd suggest anything, I'd need to know whether the ferry departure is the book's inciting event or a memory the book returns to — the opening reads as though it could be either, and that changes what it's promising.

Does the man on the ferry come back?

results.ask: Thinking about the book as a whole, what does this opening promise a reader?
results.watch: Stays at the whole; no sentence edits or line suggestions; any other level only as a closing choice.
results.reply:
Plainly: this opening promises a book about what people don't say. Mara holds something back ("She would not cry, not here"), Tomas misreads it, and a third person — whoever is at the rail — leaves without being named. A reader may come away expecting a story where the pressure sits under the surface of small actions: a cigarette lit, a minute asked for, a coat watched until it's out of sight. It also promises restraint as a method; the grief is stated as a refusal rather than shown.

The thing most at work here is how far the narration can see. You stay close to Mara for almost all of it — the water, the resolve, the coat — and then step once outside her: "Behind her, Tomas lit a cigarette and thought she was being ridiculous." That single move tells a reader the telling isn't locked inside one head; it can cross into Tomas when it wants to, and it mostly chooses not to. So the promise isn't only about these two people, it's about access — a reader may start reading every later withholding as deliberate, since they've been shown the narration could do otherwise.

results.reply:
The strongest promise here is the unnamed man. Tomas is behind her with his cigarette, so the coat at the rail belongs to someone the passage doesn't name and doesn't explain. A reader may well carry that figure forward as the thing the book owes them — who he is, why he's leaving, what Mara isn't saying about it.

A few other things the opening sets up, as I read it:

The narration can enter more than one head. "Behind her, Tomas lit a cigarette and thought she was being ridiculous" steps out of Mara without ceremony. That establishes a narrator with access to both of them, which means a reader may expect that access to be used again — and may notice if the rest of the book stays inside Mara only.

Withholding is the method. "She would not cry, not here" names a feeling and refuses it in the same breath; the unattributed dialogue is clipped to almost nothing; "The gulls kept their own counsel" makes even the setting discreet. The promise is a book where pressure is read off surfaces rather than stated. That's a real contract — if the prose later explains Mara's grief directly, it may land as a different book than this paragraph suggested.

Distance between the two people on the shore. "Thought she was being ridiculous" and "In a minute" put Tomas and Mara in completely different emotional weather, with no narration bridging them. A reader might take that gap as a line the book intends to work along.

One tension worth naming, though it's only local evidence: the departing man is given more weight than anything else in the passage, but he gets the last clause and nothing more. If he's central, the placement is doing good work. If Tomas is the book's concern and the ferry is backdrop, the final sentence may pull a reader's attention somewhere the book doesn't plan to follow.

It starts after the leaving, which is the most interesting thing it does. We never see the goodbye, the reason, or the man's face — we come in at the moment when there's nothing left to do but stand there. "She would not cry, not here" tells us there's a whole history behind this without showing any of it, and the passage seems to trust us to live without it.

The one place I'd stop is the last sentence. "She could still see the color of his coat at the rail" is where the scene's weight lands — and on a first pass a reader might take "his" as Tomas, who's the only man named and who's standing right behind her. If the man on the ferry is someone else, that ambiguity sits on the sentence doing the most work. That's not an argument for starting earlier; it might just be an argument for one word.

Before I'd suggest moving the opening, I'd need to know whether this is the first page of the book or a scene well into it, and whether the man on the ferry has been on the page before. A scene can start this far in if the reader already knows who is leaving.

results.reply:
The scene starts after the decisive event — "pull away" means the ferry is already going — so what's on the page is aftermath rather than departure. That's a defensible place to begin, and the passage seems to know it: Mara's refusal to cry, the cigarette, the flat exchange all belong to the minute after, not the moment of.

What complicates the question is the last sentence. Until "She could still see the color of his coat at the rail," nothing has told us anyone is aboard. Up to that point a reader could take the ferry as scenery and Tomas as the person she's with. The sentence that supplies the stake arrives sixth. Two readings of that, and I don't think the passage alone settles which you intend: the withholding may work as a slow reveal, where a reader re-reads the earlier lines with new weight; or a reader may spend most of the paragraph without the thing that makes the paragraph matter, and feel the pull-back more than the ache.

There's also a referent question at the end — "his" lands closest to Tomas, who is behind her, so the coat at the rail has to be reassigned mid-sentence. Whether that's a useful double-take or a stumble depends on how much you want the reveal to cost.

If you wanted the stake earlier, the smallest move is not restructuring but a single word in the first line that puts a person on the boat; it would gain orientation and lose the late turn. Leaving it is equally live.

results.ask: How does the last sentence move?

results.reply:
It turns the scene around. Everything before it has her facing away or being approached from behind — the ferry pulling off, Tomas at her back with his cigarette, the gulls above. The last sentence sends her attention back out across the water and lands on one fixed point, the rail, while everything in that direction is leaving. The sentence itself holds still; the thing it's looking at doesn't.

Two other things it's doing. *Still* carries time in it — it suggests she's been looking longer than the paragraph has shown us, and that the looking is a kind of holding on. And *his* doesn't resolve on first pass: Tomas is the only man named, but he's behind her, so the coat has to belong to someone else, someone the passage never names. A reader might have to go back a line to work that out. That reach may be the point — it keeps the person who actually matters out of the frame — but it's worth knowing you've asked for it.

And it pairs with the second sentence without repeating it. The water gets pinned to an exact shade, old pewter. The coat is only said to have one; we never learn which. You tell us she can see it and not what she sees. That withholding sits well against *She would not cry, not here.*

Do you want *his* to land straight away, or are you content for a reader to double back for it?

results.reply:
It moves away from her. The sentence begins with Mara ("She"), travels through the edge of what she can still make out, and lands on "at the rail" — a place she isn't, on something that's leaving. So the grammar goes in the same direction as the ferry.

The idea underneath that is end-position. Whatever a sentence puts last tends to be where attention settles and stays, so a sentence can end on the thing closest to the speaker or the thing furthest from her, and the reader's eye follows. Here the last four words hand the reader a man who hasn't been named — "his" isn't Tomas, who is behind her with a cigarette — so the close of the passage opens onto someone the reader hasn't met, out on the water, about to be too far to see. "Still" does time-work in the same breath: it means both *even now* and *not for much longer*.

The thing I'd flag first: that sentence is carrying an echo. "the colour of old pewter" and "the color of his coat at the rail" use the same construction, and together they suggest Mara is a person who registers colour when she won't register anything else. If you compress the second sentence to a direct metaphor — "The water was old pewter" — you gain two words and lose the pairing. Whether that's a cost depends on whether the echo is deliberate.

If you do want it tighter, the options differ by what they give up:

- **The water was pewter.** Tightest. "Old" is doing work, though — tarnish, dullness, something handled a long time — and pewter alone is just a metal.
- **Leave it.** Worth noting it isn't actually one of the long sentences here; two others run to twelve words. The slowness you may be feeling could be the flat was/was/was spine across the opening rather than the length of this one line.

As I read it, the paragraph isn't arguing that the muscle idea is wrong. It's arguing that our confidence in it has outrun what the evidence can hold up. That's what "seemed to prove it" and "far less tidy" do — they pull back from certainty without replacing it with a counter-claim.

Two other things I notice in these three sentences. The turn starts earlier than you might expect: "seemed" already tips the reader before the third sentence spells it out, so the last sentence confirms a suspicion rather than delivering a surprise. And the blame lands in a specific place — not on us for believing it, not on the original researchers, but on "the bestsellers." That word arrives only at the very end, and it quietly changes who the paragraph is against.

Whether that's what you want depends on what follows. If the next paragraph goes after popular science writing, the ending is doing setup work. If it goes back to the research itself, the bestsellers may read as a passing swipe.

results.watch: Answers the argument; any move to another level appears only as a closing choice, never "you should".
results.reply:
Plainly: it's arguing that a widely held belief rests on shakier evidence than people assume. Notice what it doesn't claim — it never says willpower isn't a muscle. It says the studies that seemed to show it haven't held up on repetition, and that the popular version is tidier than the actual record. The subject of the argument is the state of the evidence, not the nature of willpower.

The thing doing most of the work is the sequencing in time: believe, then seemed to prove, then since then. Each sentence revises the one before it, so the reader arrives at the doubt by following a chronology rather than being handed a verdict. And seemed is the hinge — it lets the second sentence stand up the claim while already withdrawing support from it, so the third sentence lands as confirmation rather than contradiction. The stronger conclusion, that the muscle idea is wrong, is left for the reader to reach or not reach on their own.

results.watch: Answers the argument; any move to another level appears only as a closing choice, never "you should".
results.reply:
It's arguing about the standing of a belief rather than about willpower itself. The three sentences run: here's what we take for granted, here's what seemed to license it, here's why that licence is weaker than assumed. The conclusion the words actually reach is the second half of sentence three — the picture is less tidy — not that the muscle model is wrong.

A few things the wording does precisely. *Seemed to prove* puts the 1990s studies at arm's length without yet saying they were mistaken. *Many attempts* and *have failed* is the only hard, checkable claim in the paragraph; everything else is framing around it. And the final target is *the bestsellers*, which shifts the critique one step away from the research and onto its popularization — so the paragraph can hold the science as unsettled while holding the popular account as overconfident. Those are two different charges, joined by a single *and*.

*Most of us* also does structural work: it enlists the reader into the belief before unsettling it, so the correction lands as shared rather than as a rebuke. A reader might feel caught out by that, or included in the revision — the words support either.

What the paragraph withholds is any positive claim about what willpower is. If this opens a chapter, that withholding reads as setup. If it's meant to carry the argument on its own, the load sits on *far less tidy*, which is evaluative rather than evidential.
